source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), no examples, matched or beat UCLA students on a new text matrix task (Digit Matrices).
numbers: Digit Matrices, 40 students: GPT-3 beat humans when generating (OR=1.88, p=0.005) and when choosing among options (OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8). Best student got every item right.
limits: Authors admit they cannot rule out training-data overlap for other tasks. Later work (Lewis and Mitchell, Hodel and West) disputes generality.
agent_relevance: Raw LLMs can score well on relation-pattern tasks without any mapping scaffold; do not assume a mapping scorer is needed for simple patterns.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 showed human-like difficulty signatures on matrices: relation rules (progression) harder, more distinct rules harder, spatially permuted elements harder.
numbers: Progression vs not: humans OR=0.41, GPT-3 OR=0.07. Unique rules: humans OR=0.61, GPT-3 OR=0.25. Permuted vs aligned logic: humans OR=0.52, GPT-3 OR=0.06. Profile correlation r(30)=0.39, p=0.027.
limits: GPT-3 effects were stronger than human effects, so it is more brittle to alignment and relation type.
agent_relevance: Alignment (shared structure shown in parallel) helps the model more than people. Present source and target in aligned, parallel form.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogies (Gentner, Rattermann and Forbus materials): both GPT-3 and students preferred the target story sharing causal (higher-order) relations. This is the direct systematicity test. GPT-3 was weak on far (cross-domain) analogies.
numbers: Combined: GPT-3 binomial p=0.0005; humans t(53)=21.3 (N=54). Near: GPT-3 p=0.0039. Far: GPT-3 p=0.065 (not significant), humans t(53)=16.7. Students beat GPT-3 (OR=0.37, p=0.0003); 15/54 students were right on every trial.
limits: Near = same entities; far = different entities. GPT-3 only. Few problems per condition.
agent_relevance: Systematicity preference (causal chain over matching first-order facts) is visible in LLMs for near cases, weak for far cases. A scaffold must force cross-domain relation matching.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Initial GPT-4 test on the same story-analogy items was much stronger than GPT-3.
numbers: GPT-4 near analogy nearly perfect; far analogy above chance (two-sided binomial p=0.0039).
limits: Only reported in the supplement as an initial test; no matched human N for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Stronger models close much of the far-analogy gap; model choice matters more than prompt for this paradigm.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Semantic distance effect: GPT-3, like people, did worse when the A:B and C:D terms were semantically far apart.
numbers: Jones et al. dataset: GPT-3 OR=3.24 for semantic distance, p=0.0165, CI [1.24, 8.5].
limits: One dataset.
agent_relevance: Surface closeness still biases the model; far mappings need explicit relation naming.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Counterfactual letter-string analogies (permuted alphabets, symbol alphabets): humans stay accurate, GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 fall sharply.
numbers: Overall accuracy across all alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773]; the three models 0.488, 0.350, 0.452 (the PDF text layout leaves the model-to-number mapping slightly uncertain, but all are far below humans). Humans 1,876 samples, each model 6,840.
limits: Task has no single right answer. Counting letters in permuted alphabets is a confound (Webb et al. 2024 reply).
agent_relevance: LLM mapping quality depends on how familiar the relation vocabulary is. Map on abstract relations explicitly, not on remembered surface patterns.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Partial failed replication of the human-matching claim on the original (non-permuted) problems: GPT models were generally below human average, unlike Webb et al.
numbers: Zero-generalization setting: 70 samples per problem type for their GPT runs vs 100 for Webb; differences noted on Predecessor, Fix Alphabet, Remove Redundant, Sort. Their humans scored higher than Webb's humans (46 and 57 samples per problem type).
limits: Different prompts and protocol can explain part of the gap.
agent_relevance: Report results with the exact prompt; a large swing can come from protocol alone.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Error analysis: GPT-4 finds the same literal alternative rules as people, but does not produce the more inventive alternative rules; GPT-4 also makes wrong-rule and over-long outputs that humans rarely make.
numbers: About 160 incorrect answers per GPT model and 184 human errors were hand-coded into four categories.
limits: Manual coding, small samples.
agent_relevance: Models can pick a valid but shallow mapping. A scoring step should compare candidate mappings, not accept the first one.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Counterfactual comprehension check: models mostly understood the fictional alphabet, so failure is not simple misunderstanding of the setup.
numbers: GPT-4 successor/predecessor on permuted letters 0.93-1.00 on most cells; GPT-3.5 predecessor only 0.49 at n=2 permuted (unpermuted pairs). GPT-3 successor 0.76-0.85 on unpermuted pairs for n=2..10.
limits: Check only tests single-letter facts.
agent_relevance: Always run a comprehension check on the representation before judging the mapping.

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Argues Webb et al.'s items may be in training data and that human tests may not measure LLM ability; simple variations broke GPT-3 while human performance stayed high.
numbers: On their reruns only Remove Redundant and Sort stayed in the original accuracy range. Comprehension check: GPT-3 kept at least 30% of its original accuracy in all but one case (predecessor, synthetic alphabet).
limits: Pre-print response; GPT-3 only; small variations.
agent_relevance: Treat any mapping win on public paradigms as possibly contaminated. Test on fresh relations.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Reply: GPT-4 with code execution solved the shuffled-alphabet letter-string analogies at human level; without code it did worse. Authors blame counting, not analogy.
numbers: Interval-size effect: humans P=1.5e-11, GPT-4 P<2e-16, GPT-4+code P=0.066. GPT-4 vs humans P=8.9e-13; GPT-4+code vs humans P=0.496. Humans N=99 (interval 1), N=97 (interval 2). 46% (23/50) of GPT-4 errors were valid alternative rules vs 39% of human errors.
limits: Code execution is not a human-like solution. Accuracy was hand-graded.
agent_relevance: A tool (code) fixed an index-counting failure. This fits our schema: code does the counting and checking, the model does the relation reasoning.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Re-representation tasks (words mapped to symbol patterns, e.g. adult/juvenile to upper/lower case). Best LLMs reach human level but behave differently on controls: they depend on example order and are hurt by irrelevant semantic distractors.
numbers: Permuted Pairs: accuracy drop significant for Claude 3 (coef -1.78, p<0.001), GPT-4 (-1.68, p<0.001), Llama-405B (-2.34, p<0.001); humans unaffected. Distracted condition: all subject types drop about 0.25. Humans match reference 0.4-0.9 across conditions; best LLMs 0.1-0.95. Older models in Defaults: GPT-3 0.5, Claude 2 0.6, Falcon 40B 0.1, Pythia-12B 0.0.
limits: Reference-match, not accuracy, since analogies have no single right answer. Humans from Brown students and Prolific.
agent_relevance: Shuffle example order and add a distractor row as a stress test for any mapping step; if the answer flips, do not trust it (guardrail G3).

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Study 2, semantic content: Claude 3 matched humans; GPT-4 and Llama-405B were much worse. Best model beat humans on compositional (two-attribute) variants where humans were weakest.
numbers: Human and Claude 3 about 0.70 reference match; GPT-4 and Llama-405B about 0.35. GPT-4 vs humans coef -1.37, p=0.002; Llama-405B -1.26, p=0.004; Claude 3 vs humans coef 0.21, p=0.64.
limits: Model differences are large, so one model is not 'LLMs'.
agent_relevance: Mapping skill varies by a factor of two across models; measure it per model before trusting the mapping step.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Frames structure mapping theory's gap: it assumes relations are already given in predicate form and does not say how the right relations are found (re-representation). Copycat, BART, and program-induction models handle this only in narrow domains.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Chalmers, French, Hofstadter 1992 for the criticism and Hofstadter and Mitchell 1995 for Copycat.
quote: SMT largely sidesteps the question of how appropriate representations are constructed
limits: Their own summary of the field, not a test.
agent_relevance: Our agent's systematicity score must run after a step that extracts relations; the LLM is a plausible extractor, the scorer should be code.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Benchmark built from system mappings (relational system) versus surface mappings, crossing near/far analogies with near/far disanalogies. LLMs see near analogies fine but fail far analogies where surface cues mislead.
numbers: 1096 triples. Zero-shot accuracy (near-far | near-near | far-far | far-near | avg): GPT-4 94.0, 92.5, 57.1, 29.1 | 68.1; GPT-3.5 60.3 avg; SBERT 42.3 avg; Llama-2-7B 53.7; FlanT5-xxl 64.4; humans 98.6, 97.2, 96.8, 91.4 | 96.0. Random is 50.
quote: even the largest ones struggle with far analogies in a zero-shot setting, with GPT4.0 scoring below random
limits: Last partitions have a surface-similar disanalogy as distractor; GPT-4 29.1% there is below random. Proverb-based narratives only.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that without scaffolding the model picks the surface-similar story over the systematically mapped one. Scoring mapping structure must override surface similarity.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6% on average (worse than random). Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. Embedding similarity alone (SBERT) already gets 77.9% on near analogies.
numbers: Averages over the model set tested; human numbers from a small human study.
limits: Averages mix very different model sizes.
agent_relevance: Embedding similarity is a surface proxy and fails exactly where systematicity matters.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Scaffolds: solved demonstrations helped far analogies and hurt near ones. Chain-of-thought demonstrations (first extract each narrative's high-level message, then choose) helped far analogies most.
numbers: CoT demonstrations gave GPT-based models gains of up to 30 absolute points on far analogies versus zero-shot. Demonstrations from far analogies were slightly more helpful than near ones. 2, 4, 6 demonstrations tested. Near-analogy accuracy fell with both plain and CoT demonstrations (less with CoT).
limits: Best few-shot model was only about halfway between random and humans. GPT-4 not tested in every ablation (cost).
agent_relevance: A two-step scaffold (extract abstract relational message first, then compare) is what helped. Fits our pipeline: make relation extraction an explicit slot.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: a novel benchmark for long text analogy evaluation in LLMs
finding: Benchmark with six levels (word, word vs sentence, syntactic, negation, entailment, metaphor) over 13 datasets and 8 LLMs, using embedding-space analogy tests.
numbers: Finding stated in abstract: identifying analogies gets harder as one climbs the taxonomy. No single accuracy figure extracted.
limits: Embedding vector-offset test, not generation or prompting; per-model scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: Vector offsets capture word-level relations but degrade for higher-level relational structure, so do not use embedding cosine as the systematicity score.

source: Sultan and Shahaf (2022) Life is a Circus and We are the Clowns: automatically finding analogies between situations and processes
finding: Non-LLM system that builds an SME-style relational mapping from plain procedural text (no hand-built predicates). It extracts entities and relations with question-form representations and searches for the mapping by beam search.
numbers: Mapping correctness (top-3 beam): ProPara 0.87 precision, F1 0.76; psychology stories 0.94 precision, F1 0.84. Question-based representation (FMQ) beat verb-only (FMV): ProPara top-1 precision 0.82 vs 0.48. Finds analogies among procedural paragraphs with 79% precision (analogy prevalence in data 3%).
quote: algorithm identifies the correct mappings 87% of the time for procedural texts and 94% for stories
limits: 15 volunteer annotators on 15 paragraph pairs; no prior baseline for mappings; ProPara pairs were pre-selected by their own method, a possible bias.
agent_relevance: A working pipeline: text, then relations, then mapping with relational score. Can be copied as code with an LLM extractor in the first step.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant examples and knowledge before solving. It beats zero-shot CoT and often hand-written few-shot CoT. No structure-mapping score is used.
numbers: GSM8K (GPT-3.5-turbo): 5-shot CoT 75.0%, self-generated exemplars 75.8%, best variant 77.8%; MATH 33.0% to 37.3%. Codeforces and BIG-Bench reasoning tasks also improved. Paper summary: average gain about +4%.
limits: Gains are small on GSM8K; works only on larger models. Self-generated examples can be wrong. Table cells partly misaligned in PDF text.
agent_relevance: Cheapest analogy method in an agent loop, but it generates analogs; it does not rank them by relational depth.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Model-size boundary: self-generated exemplars help only when the base model is strong enough.
numbers: GSM8K by base model: text-davinci-002 5-shot CoT 43%, retrieved 47%, self-generated about 48%; text-davinci-003 5-shot CoT 50%, retrieved 54%, self-generated 57-61%; small models (curie-001) 2-3% for all methods.
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction; direction of effect is clear, exact cells less so.
agent_relevance: Do not add an analogy step for small models; it only adds noise.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Diverse self-generated exemplars beat non-diverse ones; self-consistency on top lifted results further.
numbers: GSM8K 77.8% (diverse) vs 75.9% (non-diverse); MATH 37.3% vs 35.2%. With self-consistency 85.3% GSM8K and 46.0% MATH.
limits: Self-consistency alone is a large confound; same-model samples are not independent (G4).
agent_relevance: Diversity of the analogs matters; pick analogs by code for structural variety.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with large language models
finding: Agent loop that proposes analogous problems, solves them, and reuses their solutions to fix the first answer. In creative writing the analogs are paraphrases of the input, not structure-mapped ones.
numbers: Creative writing coherence (GPT-4): IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.68, TP 7.99; human preference TP 45% vs ToT 33%. GPT-3.5: TP 7.00, 39% preference. ALFWorld agent planning: TP variants 83.7-94.8% vs Reflexion 79.1% and ReAct best-of-6 71%. Abstract: +12% shortest-path, +13% preference, +15% agent task completion.
limits: TP makes several solver calls, so budgets differ from baselines. GPT-4 coherence grader (model judge).
agent_relevance: Closest existing example of an analogy method inside an agent loop. Analog reuse helped with no relational scoring step, so a code-checked mapping score is untested room.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models
finding: InstructGPT can generate analogies for a target concept; quality depends on prompt style and model size. Best prompts are precise imperative statements at low temperature.
numbers: Human evaluation of 1.4k generated analogies: largest InstructGPT near human level at producing a source concept (ACG); the explanation task (AEG) lags. Size effect: 19.17% and 15.34% relative improvement from 0.3B to 1.3B. Injected spelling errors cut quality 3-7% relative.
limits: 2022 InstructGPT models, older than current ones.
agent_relevance: Analog generation is feasible, but explaining the mapping (the part systematicity scores) is the weaker step.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) AnalogyKB: unlocking analogical reasoning of language models with a million-scale knowledge base
finding: Million-scale analogy base built from knowledge graphs. Same-relation analogies come straight from the graph; analogous-relation analogies are found with LLM selection and filtering. Used to train small models.
numbers: Paper states over 95% accuracy of the filtered analogies on a 200-item human check (abstract/intro level; model-gain numbers not extracted).
limits: I read the abstract, intro and parts of the tables, not the full evaluation.
agent_relevance: A store of relation-matched analogy pairs; a possible retrieval source for base domains.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: On ConceptARC (abstraction of core concepts), neither text GPT-4 nor multimodal GPT-4V approaches human accuracy, even with detailed one-shot prompts.
numbers: Minimal tasks (48): humans 0.95, GPT-4 0.69 (temp 0) and 0.65 (temp 0.5), GPT-4V 0.25 zero-shot and 0.23 one-shot. Full corpus (from Moskvichev et al.): humans 91%, top Kaggle program 52%, GPT-4 25%.
limits: Concerns abstraction and rule induction, not systematicity directly; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Rule induction from few examples is still weak without tools; check rules by running code on held-out examples (G3).

source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Systematicity principle as summarised on Wikipedia, not the original paper: a relation inside a connected system of relations is more likely carried to the target than an isolated one. Example: the Sun-Earth temperature difference is not mapped because it has no strong ties to mapped relations such as distance, attraction, mass.
numbers: No numbers on the page. Clement and Gentner 1991 appears only in a footnote with no design or results.
limits: Secondary source only. The original 1983 and 1991 papers were not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Rule for our scorer: prefer the mapping with the deepest connected chain of relations, and carry over inferences only if they connect to it.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The structure-mapping engine
finding: SME is the classic algorithm that scores a mapping by rewarding connected structure (cited in Webb 2023 and Sultan and Shahaf).
numbers: not read
limits: Cited only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Reference algorithm for a code-based systematicity scorer.

source: Hofstadter and Mitchell (1995) Copycat
finding: Copycat explores re-representations of letter strings by mixing bottom-up and top-down processes; works only in synthetic letter-string worlds (per Musker et al. 2025).
numbers: not read
limits: Described second-hand in Musker et al. 2025; not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows why relation extraction must be re-tried when a mapping score is low.

source: Ushio et al. (2022) BERT is to NLP what AlexNet is to CV: can pre-trained language models identify analogies?
finding: Off-the-shelf language models identify word analogies only to a degree; they struggle with abstract and complex relations, and results are very sensitive to hyperparameters and architecture. GPT-2 and RoBERTa were best; BERT did not beat word embeddings.
numbers: Abstract and one result cell read (GPT-3 sPMI 34.7 on one dataset); other numbers not extracted.
limits: Word-pair analogies (SAT-style), not systems of relations.
agent_relevance: Older evidence that scoring by embedding or likelihood is brittle; use only for the 'do not score by embedding' argument.
